column4: The section's ط ع م lexicon includes tasting, and its secondary lip image includes water crowded by mouths; here soldiers drink from a river under a one-handful limit, putting the same tasting root on water and showing measured access. The verse does not say the river is depleted.
The section says one may ask another to speak and develops food and speech as two mouth-functions; here a prisoner asks Yusuf to interpret dreams that feature pressed drink and bread eaten by birds.
The section's dictionary sense joins requesting food with speech; Yusuf says he will tell the prisoners the interpretation before their food arrives, placing speech and a meal in one scene.

The section brings outward speech together with inward eating; the disciples explain that they want to eat from the heavenly table, have their hearts reassured, and know that Jesus has told them the truth.
The section's فَكُّ رَقَبَةٍ is bodily release; this alms list again names في الرقاب among the people supported by charity, alongside the poor and needy.
The section contrasts food that should nourish with consumption that turns to punishment; this ayah names food for the sinner, a direct contrary meal.
The section develops asking and giving around food; here the disciples make a spoken request for a table sent down from heaven.
This ayah is Jesus' spoken request to God for the table and its provision, completing the section's relation between a request and food given.
The section's dictionary sense of face-to-face speech is a two-way exchange; this ayah tells the person who receives a greeting to answer with a better one or return it.
The section treats outward speech as a bodily act with consequences; this ayah itself calls the marital utterance blameworthy and false, and 58:3 supplies the following neck-freeing expiation.
The section names freeing a neck as a bodily act; this ayah gives enslaved people a written path to emancipation and directs others to help them from God's provision.

The section's speaker boasts of spending abundant wealth and imagines himself beyond anyone's power; this ayah depicts the opposite money-direction, hoarding and counting wealth, yet the same false confidence that wealth can secure lasting life.

The section says unjust consumption can become fire in the belly; after 44:44 names food for the sinner, this ayah's own contribution is that it boils in the bellies, reversing food's nourishing role.

The section's dictionary water image is a source crowded by people; this ayah places a crowd watering flocks at the water of Midian while two women wait apart. It does not say people drink or that the water is exhausted, so the parallel is limited to a shared gathering at a water source.

The section's dictionary image has mouths seeking water; this ayah asks about the water people drink and who sends it from the clouds. It gives a concrete drinking-and-provision parallel, but does not mention crowding or depletion.
